issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may not use its general appellate power to remove a payment condition from a decree when the respondent did not specifically challenge that condition in a cross-objection and paid no court fee on the relevant amount.
material_facts: The plaintiff was a party to the defendant’s appeal and filed a cross-objection limited to costs and mesne profits.
The cross-objection did not challenge the trial court’s requirement that the plaintiff pay the defendant before recovering possession.
The plaintiff paid no court fee on the amount whose repayment was a condition of obtaining possession.
The High Court nevertheless altered that condition under its general appellate power.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to remove the payment condition; the plaintiff was not entitled to that relief without a specific ground in the cross-objection and payment of court fees on the amount.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 41 Rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the appellate court could not grant the plaintiff relief removing the payment condition in these circumstances. The Supreme Court distinguished the cases relied on by the High Court and cited no other earlier case as the basis for this ruling.

rule.if: civil_appeal and respondent_filed_cross_objection and payment_condition_not_challenged_in_cross_objection and court_fee_not_paid_on_relevant_amount

predicates.civil_appeal: The matter is an appeal in a civil proceeding.
predicates.respondent_filed_cross_objection: The respondent in the appeal filed a cross-objection.
predicates.payment_condition_not_challenged_in_cros: The respondent’s cross-objection did not challenge the condition requiring payment before obtaining the requested relief.
predicates.court_fee_not_paid_on_relevant_amount: The respondent did not pay court fees on the amount relevant to removing the payment condition.
predicates.relief_removing_payment_condition_unavai: The appellate court cannot grant relief removing the payment condition.

issues.definition: When a respondent in a civil appeal files a cross-objection but does not challenge the payment condition or pay court fees on the relevant amount, the appellate court cannot remove that condition.

issues.legal_issue: A decree cancelling an assignment should stand when the courts below were right to grant cancellation on the facts and the challenge to that decree is rejected.
material_facts: The trial court decreed cancellation of the assignment, subject to the plaintiff paying the defendant before recovering possession.
The defendant argued in the Supreme Court that cancellation should not have been decreed.
The Supreme Court considered the facts and circumstances and agreed that the courts below were right to grant cancellation.
issues.conclusion: The decree cancelling the assignment stands.
issues.legal_principle: The Supreme Court concluded on the facts and circumstances that the courts below were right to grant cancellation. It cited no statutory provision or earlier case as the basis for this conclusion.

predicates.appeal_challenges_cancellation_decree: An appeal challenges a decree cancelling an assignment.
predicates.lower_courts_granted_cancellation: The lower courts granted cancellation of the assignment.
predicates.cancellation_decree_found_correct_on_the: The appellate court finds on the facts that the cancellation decree was correctly granted.
predicates.cancellation_decree_upheld: The decree cancelling the assignment is upheld.

issues.definition: If an appeal challenges a cancellation decree granted below and the appellate court finds that decree correct on the facts, the cancellation decree is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: A defendant required to deliver possession only after the plaintiff pays a specified amount is not liable for mesne profits before payment, but may be liable from payment if possession is not then delivered.
material_facts: The trial court ordered the defendant to deliver possession only upon the plaintiff paying the specified amount.
The High Court directed an inquiry into mesne profits from the date of suit.
The Supreme Court held that the defendant could not be liable for mesne profits before the plaintiff paid the amount required for possession.

The parties disputed whether the defendant remained in possession; the Supreme Court directed that, if needed, the first court determine that dispute in a proceeding to assess mesne profits after payment.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s mesne-profits decree was modified: liability could begin only from the date of payment, and only if the defendant failed to deliver possession after payment. Whether possession had been delivered was left for determination by the first court if necessary.
issues.legal_principle: Where a decree makes delivery of possession conditional on payment, the defendant cannot be liable for mesne profits before that payment. If payment is made and possession is not delivered, mesne profits may be assessed from the date of payment. The Court relied on the condition in the trial court’s decree and cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this ruling.

rule.if: possession_recovery_proceeding and decree_conditions_possession_on_payment and payment_made and possession_not_delivered_after_payment

predicates.possession_recovery_proceeding: The proceeding seeks recovery of possession of property.
predicates.decree_conditions_possession_on_payment: The decree requires payment before the claimant is entitled to possession.
predicates.payment_made: The claimant has made the payment required by the decree.
predicates.possession_not_delivered_after_payment: The person required to deliver possession has not done so after payment.
predicates.mesne_profit_liability_begins_only_on_pa: Any liability for mesne profits begins no earlier than the date of payment.

issues.definition: When a possession decree requires payment first, mesne-profit liability can begin only from payment if possession is not delivered afterward.
